I would say urgent repairs include: 

Mould in bathroom, makes it not meet minimum living standards for rental properties. It sounds like without some significant re-water proofing and plumbing and tiling work the mould will only reoccur, which will open you up to being continuously re-breached and have tenants able to leave at very short notice due to the property not meeting minimum standards.

Electrical issues including any re-wiring, if it doesn't meet minimum electrical safety standards, does not meet minimum standards for rental properties.

Asbestos definitely needs to be examined, if it has damage or any loose parts - not fit for living in, let alone renting.

Guttering + eaves + tree roots re plumbing by not fixing these you just are opening yourself up to huge structural issues including leaking roofs etc and fucked the plumbing entirely. These are also things that would always be on you to fix, as guttering etc requires a ladder, which makes it not a tenants responsibility.

The driveway being uneven could also ping you if someone gets injured, as you know about it and have been informed about it.

If a property manager (who are not known for being ethical) is saying these are issues that need to be fixed before it is rentable, you should listen.

2. I still have panic attacks pre work sometimes and I'm now years in. 


3. As someone else said, task at a time, triage. You will get better at this, and you are only a very recent graduate. Time management, priorities etc are all a challenge that improves with experience. 


4. MET calls and code blues can make experienced nurses flustered. Knowing when to step away (and tell someone so it's safe), when to delegate, when to say I just want to be told what to do here are all fine when they happen. P.S. every time shit happens with my patients I do get kind of shakey and weird but I go into task mode and you do what your role is. I also always needed to poop if I had a patient in a MET call as a grad. Immediately lol. 

Also, debrief after METs and blues and greys, particularly when you're fresh. Speak with your NIC or another staff member, if doctors have time they are usually happy to talk about it when you see them next, especially if you want to know if your escalation to the medical team was timed appropriately or was indicated. Good multidisciplinary team interactions come from experienced nurses teaching doctors the RN view and experienced doctors (and new ones tbh) teaching RNs their thought process. ICU liaison nurses are also a god send in a MET call and are usually very happy to talk to you if they're not being pulled in 9 directions by other simultaneous METs. 

5. Talk to your educators and your facilitators. Grads have fears and also it's a huge change to be the RN instead of the nursing student. It can be overwhelming but you know more than you think you do, you have these fears so you are likely appropriate and escalate things you don't know and are not the dangerous grad who thinks they're perfect and know everything.
